title: What is a body farm?
summary: Josh and Chuck visit the University of Tennessee's Forensic Anthropology Facility, known as the "body farm," in Knoxville, and discuss how outdoor human decomposition research is used in forensic science. They cover the three U.S. body farms (Tennessee, Western Carolina University, Texas State University in San Marcos), founder Dr. Bill Bass and why he started it, the stages of decomposition (flies, maggots, corpse fauna, bloating, skin slippage or "degloving," which can be used for fingerprinting), how forensic anthropologists estimate sex, age, and ancestry from skeletons, disease safety, body donation, and cases where the research helped: John Wayne Gacy's victims, the Big Bopper's death, and the 1980s-era San Diego cold case of Delbert Apodaca. The episode ends with listener mail about a bright flash of light that passed through a house during a storm.
topics: University of Tennessee Forensic Anthropology Facility

segments.title: Opening banter and visit to the body farm
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode on the University of Tennessee campus in Knoxville, near the body farm. Chuck steps in a decomposing corpse, and they joke about the setting and the article Tom wrote.

segments.title: What a body farm is and the three US locations
segments.summary: The hosts explain that body farms are outdoor research sites for studying decomposition. They list the three in the US: University of Tennessee, Western Carolina University, and Texas State University in San Marcos. They note the regional differences in decay from climate.

segments.title: Origins of the Tennessee body farm with Bill Bass
segments.summary: Dr. Bill Bass founded the Tennessee facility after police repeatedly asked him for help with murder investigations and he saw how little was known about decomposition. The first bodies were unclaimed corpses from local morgues. The site is about three acres within a larger wooded area.

segments.title: Insects, flies, and maggots as time-of-death evidence
segments.summary: Flies lay eggs in bodies within about a day, and the larvae grow quickly. Their size and stage help estimate how long a body has been exposed. Different flies arrive at different stages, forming a succession of insects called corpse fauna.

segments.title: Putrefaction, skin discoloration, and degloving
segments.summary: The hosts describe bloating, blackening skin, and lividity. They explain degloving, where the epidermis slips off a hand and can be placed on a gloved hand to take fingerprints when the fingertips are gone.

segments.title: Skeletal analysis: sex, age, ancestry, and CSI myths
segments.summary: When only bones remain, forensic anthropologists estimate sex from bone size, the forehead, chin, and pelvic inlet. Ribs indicate age. Ancestry is broadly African, Asian, or European. The hosts also say many TV forensic techniques, like blood spatter, handwriting, and gel shooting, are sensationalized.

segments.title: Disease safety and body donation
segments.summary: Residents worry about disease, but the hosts say pathogens do not persist after decomposition, and staff are vaccinated and donated bodies are screened for infectious disease. People can arrange to donate their bodies to a body farm, and the Tennessee facility had about 300 donations.

segments.title: Fun fact: skeletons versus Asian students at UT
segments.summary: Josh shares that in 2006 the University of Tennessee had more corpses and skeletons on campus than Asian students enrolled, with about 900 skeletons in one collection, 700 more in two other collections, and about forty bodies on the farm, against 673 Asian students.

segments.title: John Wayne Gacy case and identifying victims
segments.summary: Gacy's victims were buried under his mother's apartment house. After his arrest he led police to the site, and police used ground-penetrating radar. Forensic anthropologists helped identify most of the bones, which were tangled together.

segments.title: Big Bopper remains and the Delbert Apodaca cold case
segments.summary: Dr. Bass examined the remains of J.P. Richardson, the Big Bopper, at the request of his son, who wanted to know whether his father died in the 1959 plane crash. The body was found about forty feet from the plane, and the examination showed fatal crushing injuries. Next, the hosts describe a San Diego cold case of a seven-year-old, Delbert Apodaca, found in the bay, where a forensic anthropologist reviewed old photos and notes and reportedly found no evidence of sexual assault or murder as earlier concluded.

segments.title: Future decomposition guide and smell of decay
segments.summary: A researcher at Tennessee is compiling an illustrated reference atlas of decomposition for police to compare with crime scene bodies. Tom described the smell as pungent and sweet.

segments.title: Listener mail: bright flash through a house
segments.summary: Paloma from California writes about a bright white-blue flash that passed through her mother's house during a drizzly day, followed by thunder about thirty seconds later. The hosts say they can't explain it and suspect lightning, though lightning passing through a room seems unlikely. They invite listeners to send explanations.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts ask listeners to email stuffpodcasts@howstuffworks.com with explanations and point to the HowStuffWorks website for more information.
